title: Living ashtpadi 10
hookLine: seeing the countless makes our worries smaller
tomorrow: Ashtpadi 11, salok: the doer of all

lines: TWO IN THE MORNING, ONE WORRY.
THE WORRY FINDS ITS REAL SIZE.
cards: It's two in the morning, and a worry has taken over the whole room. An email you shouldn't have sent. A bill.
A test result. Lying in bed, it feels like the biggest thing in the universe. Then you get up for water, glance out the window, and there, if the sky is clear, are the stars.
More than you can count, and more behind those. The worry doesn't vanish. But it shrinks, a little, to its real size.
Astronomers didn't invent that feeling, and neither did poets. Ashtpadi ten knew it too.

teach.b: After counting the seekers and the lost, ashtpadi ten widens further. Its drumbeat, kaee kot, many millions, moves from people to worlds.
One stanza says: many millions are the sources of life and the regions of the earth. Many millions are the skies and the brahmands.
Brahmand is a universe, a whole world-system. Many millions of universes.
Guru Nanak said something similar in Japji, which we read last year: worlds below worlds, hundreds of thousands of skies above skies, and people grow tired searching for the limit.
The Granth isn't giving an astronomy lesson here. It's giving a sense of scale: vast, uncountable, beyond any edge anyone can find. So what does living this mean?
Put simply: seeing the countless makes our worries smaller. Not unimportant.
Smaller. Your worry is real, and it's yours, and in Sukhmani's picture the Creator of many millions of universes holds it too. But it's not the center of everything.
That's the gift of ashtpadi ten. It takes you outside on a clear night and says: look how big this is, look how much is being held, and see what size your worry really is.

how: Sikhs read the 'kaee kot' stanzas of Sukhmani Sahib, and Japji's lines on countless worlds, as hymns of wonder that put personal troubles in the setting of a vast creation.

o: the realm where God alone lives
the night sky over the earth

p: worlds below worlds, skies above skies
give a worry its real size

s: ashtpadi ten speaks of many millions of universes
kaee kot akaas brahmand: many millions of skies and universes.
Japji also speaks of skies above skies
worlds below worlds, skies above skies, and searchers tire of looking for the limit.
seeing the countless makes worries unimportant
not unimportant: smaller, their real size, and still held.

games.q: it's 2 a.m. and one worry fills the room. by ashtpadi ten, what helps?
o: look at the countless skies and let the worry find its size.
games.why: seeing the countless makes our worries smaller: real, held, but not the center of everything.

practice: If it's night, step outside or go to a window; if it's day, close your eyes and picture the darkest, clearest sky you've ever seen, and let your eyes go from one star to the next, knowing there are more behind each one.
Let one worry come into your mind, place it under that sky, and notice its size now. If you pray, you can hand it over to the One who holds the many millions.

wordCard.voice: Brahmand, a universe, a whole world-system. Many millions of brahmands and skies: seeing the countless gives our worries back their real size.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: brahmand, a universe, a whole world-system; ashtpadi ten counts them by the millions.

carryVoice: Your line: smaller worries. Real, and held, but not the center of everything. Sleep well.
